claim: In the RNS System pivotal RCT (n=191), responsive cortical stimulation reduced seizures by 37.9% vs 17.3% with sham over the 12-week blinded period (p=0.012).

bibliographic_record.authors: Morrell MJ, RNS System in Epilepsy Study Group.
bibliographic_record.title: Responsive cortical stimulation for the treatment of medically intractable partial epilepsy.

supporting_passage: A total of 191 adults with medically intractable partial epilepsy were implanted with a responsive neurostimulator connected to depth or subdural leads placed at 1 or 2 predetermined seizure foci. [...] Seizures were significantly reduced in the treatment (-37.9%, n = 97) compared to the sham group (-17.3%, n = 94; p = 0.012) during the blinded period

passage_location: Abstract (structured where labelled) of PMID 21917777, retrieved 2026-10-31 from Europe PMC REST API (resultType=core) = PubMed abstract; full text NOT read. Snapshot attached.

population_and_design.design: multicenter double-blind sham-controlled RCT (1:1), 12-week blinded period then 84-week open label
population_and_design.population: adults, medically intractable partial (focal) epilepsy, 1-2 seizure foci, failed >=2 AEDs, >=3 seizures/month (per abstract classification statement)

endpoint.measure: mean/GEE percent change in disabling seizure frequency vs baseline (abstract does not state median)
endpoint.follow_up_months_reported: blinded 3 months; total 2 years in open label (results reported in Heck 2014)

reported_observation: Numbers above are as reported by authors in the abstract; none re-derived except where explicitly marked 'computed'.
author_inference: Authors infer RNS reduces disabling partial seizures and is well tolerated; Class I evidence for a 12-week effect.

contradictions: Blinded endpoint is <12 months; protocol follow-up requirement met only by the open-label phase (see Heck 2014, same family).
